functional.text: Creators upload videos (up to hours long, many GB); uploads resume after a dropped connection.
Uploads are transcoded into several resolutions and formats, with thumbnails, and then published.
Viewers stream videos on any device and network; quality adapts to bandwidth.
Watch page shows title, description, channel, thumbnails and view counts.
Search videos by title, tags and channel.

non_functional.text: Playback starts in < 2 s and rarely rebuffers, worldwide.
Highly available viewing (99.99%); a few minutes to publish and seconds of search lag are fine.
Durable: an uploaded original is never lost.
Cost-efficient: egress (~80 Tbps) and storage dominate the bill.

assumptions.text: 800M DAU × 5 views = 4B views/day, ~10 min average watch at ~3 Mbps average bitrate.
500 hours uploaded per minute; ~3 GB stored per video-hour across all renditions plus the original.

out_of_scope.text: Recommendations, comments, live streaming, ads, copyright matching.

api.notes: Resume by asking how much arrived and sending the rest.
Served by CDN edges; the player picks the rendition per segment.

data.name: videos
data.fields: video_id (PK), channel_id, title, description, tags, status (uploading/processing/ready), renditions[], manifest_url, duration, created_at
data.why: Sharded by video_id; read via cache.

data.name: media objects
data.why: Immutable objects; origin for the CDN.

data.name: view_counts
data.why: Written in batches by aggregators; read with the watch page.

data.name: search docs
data.why: Inverted index fed by change events.

parts.title: Upload and transcoding pipeline
parts.problem: Accept ~500 hours of video per minute (720k hours a day), files up to hours long and many GB, and turn each into a ladder of resolutions and formats within minutes, surviving worker crashes.

options.name: transcode inside the upload request
options.cons: an hour-long video holds a connection for hours; a crash loses everything; no scaling

options.name: one job per video on one worker, renditions in sequence
options.cons: a 3-hour 4K video takes many hours; a crash restarts the whole job; workers sized for the biggest file

options.name: split into GOP-aligned segments; a DAG orchestrator fans out segment × rendition tasks over a queue to stateless workers, then packages
options.pros: minutes of latency regardless of length; retry a 10 s segment, not a video; cheap preemptible workers
options.cons: an orchestrator to run; segment boundaries and stitching must be exact

parts.choice: Resumable chunked upload to object storage, then a per-video DAG: split → encode (segment × rendition, in parallel) → package (HLS/DASH manifests) + thumbnails → publish
parts.why: 720k hours a day at ~10 core-hours per video-hour is ~300k cores, so the work must be fine-grained and retryable on cheap capacity. Segment-level tasks make publishing time roughly independent of length, and a crash costs one segment. The original is stored durably before anything else (N3).

parts.title: Storage and CDN delivery with adaptive bitrate
parts.problem: Serve ~28M concurrent streams (~80 Tbps) worldwide with playback starting in under 2 s and few stalls, on networks from 2G phones to fibre TVs.

options.name: progressive MP4 from our own origin servers
options.cons: 80 Tbps from a few data centres is impossible; far-away viewers stall

options.name: one bitrate per video through a CDN
options.cons: too big for phones on weak networks, too blurry for TVs; stalls when bandwidth drops

options.name: HLS/DASH: 2–6 s segments in a bitrate ladder, served from CDN edges with an origin shield; the player picks the rendition per segment
options.pros: starts low and climbs; adapts to every bandwidth change; segments are perfect cache objects
options.cons: many renditions to store; manifests and cache keys to manage

parts.choice: Adaptive bitrate streaming (HLS/DASH segments, 240p–4K ladder) from CDN edges with an origin shield in front of object storage
parts.why: Egress dominates cost and latency. CDN edges near viewers absorb ~95%+ of bytes because views are heavily skewed to popular videos. Small immutable segments cache well, and ABR lets the player start at a low rendition (fast start, N1) and switch per segment when bandwidth changes.

parts.title: Video metadata and search
parts.problem: Serve the watch page's metadata at ~100k reads/s (peak) and let users search billions of videos by title, tags and channel, while edits and new uploads show up within a minute.

options.name: one SQL database for metadata, LIKE queries for search
options.cons: billions of rows and 100k reads/s overload one primary; LIKE can't rank or tokenize

options.name: SQL sharded by video_id behind a read-through cache; search in a separate inverted index fed by change events
options.pros: cache absorbs the read skew; the index ranks, tokenizes, handles typos
options.cons: the index lags writes by seconds; two systems to keep in sync

options.name: one NoSQL store with secondary indexes for search
options.cons: weak relevance ranking and text analysis

parts.choice: Metadata in SQL sharded by video_id with a Redis read-through cache; search in Elasticsearch, updated by an indexer consuming metadata-change events
parts.why: Reads vastly outnumber edits and concentrate on popular videos, so a cache carries most of them. Full-text relevance needs an inverted index; feeding it from events keeps the write path fast and a few seconds of search lag is acceptable (N2).

parts.title: Counting views
parts.problem: Count ~46k views/s (peak ~90k), with a viral video taking a large share, filtering bots and repeats, and show near-real-time counts without slowing playback.

options.name: UPDATE videos SET views = views + 1 per view
options.cons: a write per view on the metadata DB; a viral video's row becomes a hot lock

options.name: Redis INCR per view
options.cons: still a hot key per viral video; no dedup or bot filtering; durability on failover

options.name: view events to a stream; windowed aggregation workers dedupe and filter, then write batched increments every few seconds
options.pros: cheap, durable, absorbs spikes; fraud filtering fits naturally
options.cons: counts lag by seconds to minutes

parts.choice: View events to Kafka partitioned by video_id; aggregation workers dedupe (viewer, video, window), drop bots and write batched increments to view_counts
parts.why: Displayed counts may lag (F6 says approximate), so batching turns 46k writes/s into a few thousand. Partitioning by video_id makes each worker own its videos' counters in memory, which removes contention on viral videos.

deep_dives.title: Bitrate ladder and codecs

options.name: fixed ladder, H.264 only
options.cons: the largest files: more egress per view

options.name: per-title ladder; H.264 for all, plus VP9/AV1 for popular videos
options.pros: 30–50% fewer bytes where most views happen
options.cons: extra encode compute; more renditions to store

deep_dives.choice: Per-title ladder with H.264 for every video; re-encode to VP9/AV1 once a video crosses a popularity threshold
deep_dives.why: Egress (~80 Tbps) costs far more than compute, but only a small fraction of videos gets most views, so spending expensive encodes only on those buys most of the savings.

deep_dives.title: Popular vs long-tail content

options.name: treat every video the same: all renditions on hot storage, CDN pull on demand
options.cons: pays hot-storage prices for petabytes nobody watches; first viewers of a launch all miss

options.name: tier by popularity: pre-warm edges for expected hits, origin shield for the long tail, move cold renditions to cheaper storage and drop rarely used high renditions
options.cons: tiering jobs and on-demand re-encode for rare requests

deep_dives.choice: Popularity tiers: pre-warm CDN for big launches, origin shield for the long tail, cold renditions to infrequent-access storage after 90 days without views
deep_dives.why: Storage grows by ~2 PB a day and most of it is rarely watched after the first weeks; tiering keeps N4 under control without hurting the popular videos that drive N1.

wrapup.bottlenecks: CDN egress and cache-hit ratio (cost and start time), transcode capacity during upload spikes (queue depth, preemptible workers), hot metadata rows for viral videos (cache), the orchestrator's state store.
wrapup.failures: Worker crash: the segment task is retried (idempotent by output key). Orchestrator restart: resumes the DAG from persisted state. CDN PoP down: DNS/anycast steers to the next PoP. Metadata shard down: cached pages keep serving. Stream down: view counts lag, playback is unaffected.
wrapup.monitoring: Video start time and rebuffer ratio from player telemetry, CDN hit ratio and egress per PoP, upload success rate, upload-to-publish latency, transcode queue depth and task retries, search index lag, view-count lag.
wrapup.scale: Add transcode workers (stateless, preemptible), more CDN capacity and PoPs, metadata shards by video_id, partitions on the events stream.
wrapup.future: Live streaming (low-latency HLS), recommendations, per-device codec negotiation, edge-side ad insertion.
